title: Matt Shirvington Salary: How to Convert an Hourly Rate to Annual Pay with Casual Loading and Super
description: Learn how to convert an hourly rate to annual pay using 38-hour weeks, casual loading, and super paid on top. Apply the same method to understand the Matt Shirvington salary.
salarySummary: Assuming a 38-hour week, the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour yields an annual gross of $52,265.28, with casual loading adding 25% to $33.05 per hour.

faqs.q: How do I calculate annual salary from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours worked per week (typically 38 for full-time) and then by 52 weeks. For example, $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,265.28 per year. This is the gross annual pay before tax and super.

faqs.q: What is casual loading and how does it affect the calculation?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% paid on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. For the National Minimum Wage, the casual rate is $33.05 per hour ($26.44 × 1.25). When converting to annual, use the loaded rate in the same formula.

faqs.q: Is superannuation included in the hourly rate or paid separately?
faqs.a: Super is paid on top of the gross pay. Employers contribute 12% of ordinary earnings (up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830) in addition to the hourly rate. For a $26.44 per hour employee, super adds about $3.17 per hour, but it is not part of take-home pay.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Matt Shirvington Salary: Hourly to Annual Conversion

When you hear about the **Matt Shirvington salary**, you might wonder how an hourly rate translates to annual pay. Whether you're a casual employee, a full-time worker, or comparing job offers, the process is straightforward: multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours worked per week, then by 52 weeks. This article explains the conversion using the latest Fair Work Ombudsman and Australian Taxation Office figures, with a focus on casual loading and super paid on top.

### The Basic Formula

Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52. For a standard full-time role of 38 hours per week, this becomes:

- National Minimum Wage (from 1 July 2026): $26.44 per hour → $26.44 × 38 × 52 = **$52,265.28 per year**
- Casual rate (including 25% loading): $33.05 per hour → $33.05 × 38 × 52 = **$65,331.60 per year**

This formula assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, and no allowances. It's a starting point for understanding the **Matt Shirvington salary** or any other hourly wage.

### Casual Loading: 25% on Top

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on their base rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave (annual leave, sick leave, etc.). The Fair Work Ombudsman states that the casual minimum wage is $33.05 per hour, which is $26.44 plus 25%. When converting to annual, always apply the loading to the hourly rate first. For example, if you have a base hourly rate of $30.00, the casual rate is $37.50, and annual gross becomes $37.50 × 38 × 52 = $74,100.

**Important:** Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading into a calculator that adds loading again. Use the base rate and let the tool add the 25% if you select the casual option. Our [the timesheet](/) allows you to enter a base hourly rate and check a box to add casual loading on top.

### Superannuation: Paid on Top

Super is not part of the hourly rate. Employers must pay 12% of ordinary earnings into your super fund, on top of your gross pay. This is capped at the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year (2026–27). For the National Minimum Wage:

- Annual super = $52,265.28 × 12% = $6,271.83
- Total employer cost = $52,265.28 + $6,271.83 = $58,537.11

Super is real value but not spendable now. When comparing job offers, always separate super from take-home pay. A total remuneration package (TRP) includes super inside it, while a base salary has super paid on top. For the **Matt Shirvington salary**, if it were quoted as a package, you would need to extract the taxable salary by dividing by 1.12.

### Tax and Take-Home Pay

Tax is calculated on your gross pay (excluding super). For 2026–27, the resident tax rates are:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% on excess over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: 30% on excess over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: 37% on excess over $135,000
- Above $190,000: 45%

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (with reductions for low-income earners). For a gross annual of $52,265.28, tax would be approximately $5,092 (using the 2026–27 scale) and Medicare $1,045, giving a take-home of about $46,128. The fortnightly take-home would be roughly $1,774.

### Fortnightly Pay

Many employees are paid fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross, multiply the weekly rate by 2. For the National Minimum Wage:

- Weekly: $26.44 × 38 = $1,004.72 (close to the Fair Work figure of $1,004.90)
- Fortnightly: $1,004.72 × 2 = $2,009.44

After tax and Medicare, the fortnightly take-home is lower. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) guide for more details.

### Award Rates vs National Minimum Wage

The National Minimum Wage applies to employees not covered by an award or enterprise agreement. Most workers are covered by an award, which sets higher minimum rates. From 1 July 2026, award minimum wages increased by 4.75%. You can find your specific award rate using the [pay guides](/blog) from the Fair Work Ombudsman. The conversion formula remains the same: hourly rate × hours × 52.

### Applying to the Matt Shirvington Salary

While we don't have a precise figure for the **Matt Shirvington salary**, the method is identical. If you know his hourly rate (base or casual), you can calculate annual gross, super, and take-home. For example, if his base hourly rate were $50.00, annual gross would be $98,800 ($50 × 38 × 52), super $11,856, and take-home around $74,000 after tax. If he were casual, the rate would be $62.50 per hour, annual $123,500, and take-home higher.

### Common Pitfalls

- **Confusing base salary with package:** A $105,000 package that includes super is actually a $93,750 taxable salary (divide by 1.12). The take-home is less than a $95,000 base salary with super on top.
- **Ignoring hours:** A $100,000 salary for a 50-hour week pays less per hour than a $90,000 salary for a 38-hour week. Always compare hourly rates.
- **Forgetting casual loading:** Casual employees must receive the loaded rate. Check your award for the correct casual percentage (often 25%).

### Tools and Resources

Use our [the timesheet](/) to convert your hourly rate to annual, fortnightly, and weekly figures, with options for casual loading and super. For award-specific rates, refer to the [reference tables](/data) or the Fair Work Ombudsman's Pay and Conditions Tool. The [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page compares your salary to ABS averages.

### Summary

Converting an hourly rate to annual pay is simple: hourly × hours per week × 52. For the **Matt Shirvington salary** or any other wage, remember to add casual loading if applicable, and treat super as a separate contribution on top. Tax and Medicare reduce your take-home, but the formula gives you a clear starting point for negotiations and budgeting.
